The researchers used a high-frequency induction furnace with a maximum melting capacity of 300 kg to re-melt and balance the composition of steel scrap.
The main steel scrap materials used were low-alloy SPCC steel and duplex stainless steel S2205, which were combined and modified with ferro-alloy additions to achieve the target 17-4 PH composition.
The investment casting mold was made by dipping a wax-shaped design into a ceramic slurry and then sintering and preheating the mold prior to pouring the molten 17-4 PH alloy.
X-ray radiography of the turbine blade prototypes revealed acceptable casting quality with no major defects like porosity, cracks, or dimensional issues.
The as-cast scrap-based 17-4 PH stainless steel had a yield strength of 677 MPa, tensile strength of 677 MPa, and 9.3% elongation.
After various heat treatments, the yield strength of the scrap-based 17-4 PH ranged from 534 to 1033 MPa, tensile strength from 448 to 1018 MPa, and elongation from 2.5% to 8.1%.
The commercial 17-4 PH stainless steel had a higher yield strength of 740 MPa, tensile strength of 1070 MPa, and 16% elongation compared to the scrap-based material.

The as-cast microstructure of the scrap-based 17-4 PH consisted of a martensitic matrix with some delta ferrite, which evolved after heat treatment with the precipitation of carbides and intermetallic phases.

The researchers used a two-step etching process with Kalling's No. 2 and Murakami's reagents to reveal the martensitic structure, delta ferrite, and secondary phases in the scrap-based 17-4 PH microstructure.
The addition of Niobium (Nb) was intended to assist the formation of intermetallic precipitates that could act as nucleation sites for precipitation hardening in the scrap-based 17-4 PH alloy.
The induction melting and investment casting process allowed for flexible use of scrap materials and near-net-shape manufacturing of the intricate turbine blade geometry.
The researchers evaluated different aging temperatures (480°C, 580°C, 620°C, 760°C) and durations (1-4 hours) to optimize the heat treatment for the scrap-based 17-4 PH stainless steel.
The maximum yield strength of 1033 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 1018 MPa were achieved for the scrap-based 17-4 PH after austenizing at 1050°C and air quenching without any aging treatment.
The researchers used a commercial 17-4 PH stainless steel as a reference material to compare the mechanical properties of the scrap-based 17-4 PH alloy.
The investment casting approach enabled the production of intricate turbine blade geometries from the scrap-based 17-4 PH stainless steel.
